articles.title: Slow Fashion Sells the Story but the Weaver Sees Little Money
articles.summary: The article examines how slow fashion brands market handmade textiles like Ikat and Kantha as premium products, but the artisans behind these crafts see little financial benefit or job security. Megha Agarwal of Studio Maeve questions whether increased visibility for artisans translates to genuine dignity or merely serves as branding for businesses. The imbalance underscores broader concerns about fair wages, labour rights, and the exploitation of vulnerable craft communities in India.
articles.raw_summary: As slow fashion turns handmade cloth into a selling point, the artisans behind Ikat and Kantha have gained visibility without a matching rise in pay or security. The imbalance raises a pointed question about who profits from the story of craft. Megha Agarwal, founder of Studio Maeve, weighs whether artisan recognition delivers genuine dignity or borrowed branding.

articles.title: Saving a Handmade Textile Means Rebuilding the Buyers Who Once Prized It
articles.summary: Himroo, a centuries-old silk-and-cotton weave from Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, has nearly disappeared due to the collapse of its market and demand. Arushi Chowdhury Khanna, founder of LoomKatha, argues that reviving such crafts requires restoring the buyers and visibility rather than just preserving weaving skills. The decline of Himroo reflects broader challenges faced by traditional textile industries in India, raising questions about workforce sustainability and economic support for artisans.
articles.raw_summary: Himroo, a centuries-old silk-and-cotton weave from the city now called Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, had fallen from thousands of handlooms to none still working. Arushi Chowdhury Khanna, who founded the social enterprise LoomKatha, argues that reviving such a craft depends less on preserving skill than on rebuilding the market and the visibility that sustain it, not on the loom alone.
